claim: Large-scale measurement and manipulation of the brain using individual probe placement techniques have been severely limited by the inability to miniaturize systems for probe positioning.
source: However, large-scale measurement and manipulation of the brain using such methods have been severely limited by the inability to miniaturize systems for probe positioning.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the work in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: The presented micropositioning approach is composed of novel phase-change material-filled resistive heater micro-grippers arranged in an inchworm motor configuration.
source: Here, we present a fundamentally new, remote-controlled micropositioning approach composed of novel phase-change material-filled resistive heater micro-grippers arranged in an inchworm motor configuration.
evidence: This is a description of the device design presented in the manuscript, supported by figures and detailed methods.

claim: The microscopic dimensions, stability, gentle gripping action, individual electronic control, and high packing density of the grippers allow micrometer-precision independent positioning of many arbitrarily shaped probes using a single piezo actuator.
source: The microscopic dimensions, stability, gentle gripping action, individual electronic control, and high packing density of the grippers allow micrometer-precision independent positioning of many arbitrarily shaped probes using a single piezo actuator.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental characterization data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The multi-probe single-actuator design significantly reduces the size and weight of microdrives.
source: This multi-probe single-actuator design significantly reduces the size and weight and allows for potential automation of microdrives.
evidence: This is supported by the design description and comparison to traditional microdrives in the discussion, as well as weight measurements provided in the results.

claim: The multi-probe single-actuator design allows for potential automation of microdrives.
source: This multi-probe single-actuator design significantly reduces the size and weight and allows for potential automation of microdrives.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the electronic control capabilities demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Accurate placement of multiple electrodes into the rat hippocampus in vivo in acute and chronic preparations was demonstrated.
source: We demonstrate accurate placement of multiple electrodes into the rat hippocampus in vivo in acute and chronic preparations.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The robotic microdrive technology should enable the scaling up of many types of multi-probe applications in neuroscience and other fields.
source: Our robotic microdrive technology should therefore enable the scaling up of many types of multi-probe applications in neuroscience and other fields.
evidence: This is a forward-looking conclusion based on the demonstrated capabilities of the device.

claim: Miniaturization of mechanical, electrical, optical, and other devices has been steadily ongoing for decades, enabled by advances in manufacturing, electronics, and novel mechanical designs.
source: The miniaturization of mechanical, electrical, optical, and other devices has been steadily ongoing for decades, enabled by advances in manufacturing, electronics, and novel mechanical designs.
evidence: This is a general statement about technological trends, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tools and techniques in neuroscience have undergone tremendous progress, enabling the study of the living, behaving brain.
source: Aided by such technological advances, tools and techniques in neuroscience have undergone tremendous progress, enabling the study of the living, behaving brain (Wise et al., 1970; Wise and Najafi, 1991; Kralik et al., 2001; Wise et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2004; Wise et al., 2008; Harrison, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: A variety of electrical, chemical, and optical probes are mechanically inserted into the brain to perform in vivo measurements or perturbations in acutely or chronically implanted animals.
source: To perform in vivo measurements or perturbations in acutely or chronically implanted animals, a variety of electrical, chemical, and optical probes are mechanically inserted into the brain (McNaughton et al., 1983; Gray et al., 1995; Jog et al., 2002; Nicolelis et al., 2003; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Blanche et al., 2005; Cogan, 2008; Royer et al., 2010; Du et al., 2011; Szuts et al., 2011; Andrásfalvy et al., 2014; Berényi et al., 2014; Schwarz et al., 2014; Canales et al., 2015; Jun et al., 2017; Feiner and Dvir, 2018; Hunt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Probes must be precisely placed in the region of scientific or clinical interest, often with micron-scale accuracy, because the brain is anatomically structured into different functional regions.
source: Since the brain is anatomically structured into different functional regions, these probes must be precisely placed in the region of scientific or clinical interest, often with micron-scale accuracy.
evidence: This is based on established neuroscience knowledge about brain organization and the requirements for targeted recordings.

claim: A number of microfabricated electrodes have enabled recording from neurons localized to a single plane or column.
source: A number of microfabricated electrodes have enabled recording from neurons localized to a single plane (Maynard et al., 1997) or column (Jun et al., 2017), but for many applications multiple independently actuated electrodes are required to record neural activity in a geometry-flexible and post-implantation adjustable fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific prior work.

claim: For many applications multiple independently actuated electrodes are required to record neural activity in a geometry-flexible and post-implantation adjustable fashion.
source: A number of microfabricated electrodes have enabled recording from neurons localized to a single plane (Maynard et al., 1997) or column (Jun et al., 2017), but for many applications multiple independently actuated electrodes are required to record neural activity in a geometry-flexible and post-implantation adjustable fashion.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental requirements based on the limitations of existing technologies.

claim: Flexible-sheet array implants can record over a large area but are typically only applicable to the external surface as in cortical experiments.
source: Flexible-sheet array implants (Lu et al., 2016) can record over a large area but are typically only applicable to the external surface as in cortical experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents knowledge about the limitations of this technology.

claim: Shank-style probes are often limited in the number and density of electrodes along their length, and therefore generally require alignment during and after implantation due to tissue movement, local scarring, or cell loss.
source: Shank-style probes are often limited in the number and density of electrodes along their length, and therefore generally require alignment during and after implantation due to tissue movement, local scarring, or cell loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing probe technologies based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Highly integrated probes with dense electrodes along a larger portion of the shank can obviate the need for adjustment.
source: While highly integrated probes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021) with dense electrodes along a larger portion of the shank can obviate the need for adjustment, there are currently limitations to the three-dimensional target geometries that are realizable with these probes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific probe technologies.

claim: There are currently limitations to the three-dimensional target geometries that are realizable with highly integrated probes.
source: While highly integrated probes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2021) with dense electrodes along a larger portion of the shank can obviate the need for adjustment, there are currently limitations to the three-dimensional target geometries that are realizable with these probes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing technologies based on knowledge of their design constraints.

claim: Beyond the standard electrode types available, highly integrated probes do not exist for the wide variety of other types of electrodes or measurement/manipulation devices that have been developed.
source: Furthermore, beyond the standard electrode types available, such probes do not exist for the wide variety of other types of electrodes or measurement/manipulation devices that have been developed (Royer et al., 2010; Canales et al., 2015; Hunt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to diverse probe technologies and represents knowledge about the current state of the field.

claim: The ability to continually and independently position multiple probes remains important within experimental neuroscience.
source: For these reasons, the ability to continually and independently position multiple probes remains important within experimental neuroscience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the limitations of existing technologies described in the preceding text.

claim: A mechanical positioner, commonly termed a microdrive, is usually employed for probe placement tasks.
source: Therefore, a mechanical positioner, commonly termed a microdrive, is usually employed for such placement tasks, and its design has also undergone steady technological development and improvement over the years (Humphrey, 1970; Ainsworth and O'Keefe, 1977; Krüger, 1983; Kubie, 1984; Korshunov, 1995; Nichols et al., 1998; Venkatachalam et al., 1999; Vos et al., 1999; Szabó et al., 2001; Keating and Gerstein, 2002; Jeantet and Cho, 2003; Swadlow et al., 2005; Korshunov, 2006; Lansink et al., 2007; Tóth et al., 2007; Battaglia et al., 2009; Haiss et al., 2010; Galashan et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2012; Voigts et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations documenting the history of microdrive development.

claim: Presently available microdrives have features that limit the extent to which the number and density of probes can be scaled up.
source: However, presently available microdrives have features that limit the extent to which the number and density of probes can be scaled up.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing technologies that motivates the current work.

claim: Microdrives tend to be manually operated devices where each independent probe is assigned its own lead-screw-based positioner.
source: Microdrives tend to be manually operated devices where each independent probe is assigned its own lead-screw-based positioner.
evidence: This is a description of conventional microdrive designs based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Increasing the number of neural probes mounted in conventional microdrives often makes them complex, bulky, and heavy and also makes the practice of probe placement increasingly cumbersome and time-consuming.
source: Therefore, increasing the number of neural probes mounted in such drives often makes them complex, bulky, and heavy and also makes the practice of probe placement increasingly cumbersome and time-consuming.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional microdrives based on their design principles.

claim: Work has gone into developing motorized microdrive devices that would allow for more efficient electrophysiological data collection through parallelization and remote computer-controlled operation without human intervention.
source: Work has gone into developing motorized microdrive devices that would allow for more efficient electrophysiological data collection through parallelization and remote computer-controlled operation without human intervention (Reitboeck, 1983; Eckhorn and Thomas, 1993; Fee and Leonardo, 2001; Johnson and Welsh, 2003; Cham et al., 2005; Venkateswaran et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007; Yamamoto and Wilson, 2008; Park et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2011; Kodandaramaiah et al., 2012; Zoll et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior work on motorized microdrives.

claim: In motorized microdrive designs, each independent neural probe is assigned its own motorized positioner, which often makes the size, weight, complexity, and expense of the microdrive prohibitive and limits their ability to scale to large numbers of probes.
source: Yet, in these designs too, each independent neural probe is assigned its own motorized positioner, which often makes the size, weight, complexity, and expense of the microdrive prohibitive and limits their ability to scale to large numbers of probes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing motorized microdrives based on their design architecture.

claim: A novel, reusable, electronically controlled, densely packable, phase-change-based microgripper for holding and releasing probes of arbitrary shapes was developed.
source: First, we developed a novel, reusable, electronically controlled, densely packable, phase-change-based microgripper for holding and releasing probes of arbitrary shapes.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed description and characterization of the microgripper in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Arrays of microgrippers were arranged into an inchworm motor configuration so that a single piezo actuator can independently translate many probes over an unlimited range of travel.
source: Then we arranged arrays of microgrippers into an inchworm motor configuration so that a single piezo actuator can independently translate many probes over an unlimited range of travel.
evidence: This is supported by the design description and demonstration in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The MPSA concept allows for a significant reduction in microdrive complexity, size, weight, and cost, while still providing micron-scale independent positioning of each neural probe.
source: This multi-probe single-actuator (MPSA) concept therefore allows for a significant reduction in microdrive complexity, size, weight, and cost, while still providing micron-scale independent positioning of each neural probe.
evidence: This is supported by the design description, weight measurements, and positioning accuracy data presented in the results.

claim: The MPSA microdrive was constructed and tested while loaded with classic twisted wire tetrodes.
source: As a proof of concept, we constructed and tested the operation of this microdrive while loaded with classic twisted wire tetrodes – a widely used type of neural electrode.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental demonstrations shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Remote-controlled, independent placement of multiple tetrodes with micrometer precision into the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus in vivo in acute and chronic settings was performed.
source: We performed remote-controlled, independent placement of multiple tetrodes with micrometer precision into the CA1 region of the rat hippocampus in vivo in acute and chronic settings.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The versatility of the approach was demonstrated by independently adjusting an array of closely packed glass micropipettes.
source: We have also demonstrated the versatility of our approach by independently adjusting an array of closely packed glass micropipettes.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: A helical resistive wire coil embedded in a printed circuit board non-plated via is connected such that an electric current from a power source can be passed through the coil.
source: A helical resistive wire coil embedded in a printed circuit board (PCB) non-plated via is connected such that an electric current from a power source can be passed through the coil.
evidence: This is a description of the microgripper design shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The electronically controlled change of the gripper's temperature is achieved through Joule heating.
source: This allows for the electronically controlled change of the gripper's temperature through Joule heating.
evidence: This is based on the established physical principle of Joule heating when current passes through a resistive element.

claim: When the heater coil does not carry current, the gripper is at the ambient temperature, the PCM in the bore is in the solid state, and therefore the neural probe is 'gripped'.
source: When the heater coil does not carry current (Figure 1A), the gripper is at the ambient temperature, the PCM in the bore is in the solid state, and therefore the neural probe is 'gripped' (Barbic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the design description, Figure 1A, and a citation to prior work on PCM gripping.

claim: When the heater coil carries current, the gripper heats up, the PCM in the bore melts and goes into the liquid state, and the neural probe is 'released'.
source: When the heater coil carries current (Figure 1B), the gripper heats up, the PCM in the bore melts and goes into the liquid state. The neural probe is therefore 'released' (Barbic et al., 2017) and can be moved axially through the gripper.
evidence: This is supported by the design description, Figure 1B, and a citation to prior work on PCM gripping.

claim: Due to the microscopic dimensions of the space between the gripper and the neural probe, the PCM can be maintained in the bore through capillary action without exiting during probe motion.
source: Critically, due to the microscopic dimensions of the space between the gripper and the neural probe, the PCM can be maintained in the bore through capillary action without exiting during probe motion.
evidence: This is based on the physical principle of capillary action in microscale spaces.

claim: The gripper is operated electronically which allows for remote control.
source: First, the gripper is operated electronically which allows for remote control.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the electronic heating design and is demonstrated in the experimental results.

claim: The gripper is dimensionally microscopic (~75 μm inner diameter/110 μm outer diameter) and of similar cross-sectional size as the neural probe that it grips (twisted wire tetrode probe ~55 μm diameter).
source: Second, the gripper is dimensionally microscopic (~75 μm inner diameter/110 μm outer diameter, Figure 1C–D) and of similar cross-sectional size as the neural probe that it grips (twisted wire tetrode probe ~55 μm diameter).
evidence: This is supported by measurements and images shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The gripper takes up minimal PCB area, and many probes can be densely packed.
source: Therefore, the gripper takes up minimal PCB area, and many probes can be densely packed, as we describe in a later section.
evidence: This is an inference from the small size of the gripper and is demonstrated in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The probe gripped within the bore of the device can be of any cross-sectional shape, as the liquid PCM in the released state conforms to the probe shape before it solidifies into the gripped state.
source: Third, the probe gripped within the bore of the device can be of any cross-sectional shape, as the liquid PCM in the released state conforms to the probe shape before it solidifies into the gripped state.
evidence: This is based on the physical properties of liquid PCM and is demonstrated by gripping both tetrodes and glass pipettes.

claim: The device presents an opportunity to grip a variety of probes such as electrical testing probes, optical fibers, silicon neural electrodes, glass pipettes/capillary probes, carbon fibers, and ultrasonic probes.
source: This presents an opportunity to use the device to grip a variety of probes such as electrical testing probes, optical fibers, silicon neural electrodes, glass pipettes/capillary probes, carbon fibers, and ultrasonic probes.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the demonstrated ability to grip different probe types, with glass pipettes demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The inchworm motor is constructed from two parallel PCBs, each with the embedded helical coil heater grippers aligned along the neural probe axis.
source: The motor is constructed from two parallel PCBs, each with the embedded helical coil heater grippers aligned along the neural probe axis.
evidence: This is supported by the design description and Figure 1E.

claim: The two parallel boards are joined by a single piezoelectric block stack actuator that is controlled by a piezo actuator voltage driver.
source: The two parallel boards are joined by a single piezoelectric block stack actuator that is controlled by a piezo actuator voltage driver (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the design description, Figure 1E, and the Materials and methods section.

claim: The piezo actuator is controlled electronically which allows for remote control.
source: First, the piezo actuator is, just like the probe grippers, controlled electronically which allows for remote control.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the electronic control design and is demonstrated in the experimental results.

claim: The piezo actuator has micron-scale translation capability, accuracy, and repeatability.
source: Second, the piezo actuator has micron-scale translation capability, accuracy, and repeatability.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of piezoelectric actuators and is confirmed by the characterization data in Figure 4.

claim: The inchworm motor design allows for the long range forward or backward motion of the probe with indefinite translation range.
source: Third, the inchworm motor design in general allows for the long range forward or backward motion of the probe with indefinite translation range.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of inchworm motor designs and is demonstrated in the experimental results.

claim: The piezo can make a practically unlimited number of microscopic steps.
source: This is because the piezo can make a practically unlimited number of microscopic steps, as Figure 1F illustrates.
evidence: This is based on the principle of inchworm motors and is illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: A single downward step of the probe is performed by six inchworm motor phases.
source: A single downward step (here 9.5 µm) of the probe is performed by six inchworm motor phases (i)–(vi).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2A with detailed phase-by-phase description.

claim: Long-distance downward probe translation can be accomplished through an unlimited number of repeated single step sequences.
source: Long-distance downward probe translation can be accomplished through an unlimited number of repeated single step sequences.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the repeatable stepping mechanism shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A sequence change in the activation of the microgrippers results in a single upward step while the actuation signal to the piezo remains the same.
source: A sequence change in the activation of the microgrippers results in a single upward step. Importantly, the actuation signal to the piezo remains the same.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2B with detailed description.

claim: A no-step sequence can be applied to probes that are to remain in place while other probes are moved in a multi-probe microdrive.
source: Single no-step sequence, applied to those probes that are to remain in place while other probes are moved in a multi-probe microdrive.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2C with detailed description.

claim: In the no-step sequence, the piezo is still actuated, extending and contracting as in the up and down step sequences, but the sequence of the actuation signals to the top and bottom board heaters is such that the probe does not move.
source: The piezo is still actuated, extending and contracting as in (A) and (B), but the sequence of the actuation signals to the top and bottom board heaters is such that the probe does not move.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2C with detailed description.

claim: The availability of the three distinct probe translation operations while the piezo actuator goes through the same extension/contraction steps allows the microdrive to independently translate multiple closely packed, parallel probes while still only using a single piezo actuator.
source: The availability of the three distinct probe translation operations of the microdrive while the piezo actuator goes through the same extension/contraction steps (as described in Figure 2) allows the microdrive to independently translate multiple closely packed, parallel probes while still only using a single piezo actuator.
evidence: This is a key design principle that is demonstrated in Figure 3 and Videos 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Neural robotic microdrives with up to 16 independent helical coil heater microgrippers in each board were prepared, typically in a hexagonal closely packed array, with 300 μm center-to-center microgripper spacing.
source: We have prepared neural robotic microdrives with up to 16 independent helical coil heater microgrippers in each board, typically in a hexagonal closely packed array, with 300 μm center-to-center microgripper spacing, as shown in Figure 3D–F (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is directly supported by the description and images in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The size and weight of the microdrive remain essentially the same with the increase in the number of loaded neural probes, as the size and weight of additional probes and grippers are nearly negligible.
source: It is important to note that the size and weight of the microdrive remain essentially the same with the increase in the number of loaded neural probes, as the size and weight of additional probes and grippers are nearly negligible.
evidence: This is an inference from the design and is supported by weight measurements provided in the chronic recording section.

claim: The microgrippers must be sufficiently thermally independent to independently move the probes.
source: To independently move the probes, the microgrippers must be sufficiently thermally independent.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for independent operation that is addressed through design and testing.

claim: The close packing of probes for many applications could cause significant thermal coupling and risk unintentional probe release.
source: The close packing of probes for many applications, however, could cause significant thermal coupling and risk unintentional probe release.
evidence: This is a potential problem identified based on thermal physics principles.

claim: Simulations and translation testing revealed the importance of the short distance between a microgripper's heater and PCM relative to the distance between microgrippers and that short, controlled heat pulses would be critical.
source: Simulations and translation testing revealed the importance of the short distance between a microgripper's heater and PCM relative to the distance between microgrippers (which are separated by PCB laminate, a composite typically having low thermal diffusivity) and that short, controlled heat pulses would be critical (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by simulations and experimental testing described in the Materials and methods and Appendix.

claim: A hexagonal close packed array of 16 tetrode-sized microgrippers, with 300 μm center-to-center spacing was accomplished when the heating coils (~125 Ω) were operated with ~45 mA, yielding a ~250 mW heat output and release of the docosane-filled microgrippers in 4–12.5 ms depending on their initial temperature.
source: A hexagonal close packed array of 16 tetrode-sized microgrippers, with 300 μm center-to-center spacing was accomplished when the heating coils (~125 Ω) were operated with ~45 mA, yielding a~250 mW heat output and release of the docosane-filled microgrippers in 4–12.5 ms depending on their initial temperature.
evidence: This is directly measured operational data for the device.

claim: Heating for longer than 12.5 ms from room temperature was functionally unnecessary and risked unintentional release of adjacent grippers.
source: Heating for longer than 12.5 ms from room temperature was functionally unnecessary and risked unintentional release of adjacent grippers.
evidence: This is a conclusion from thermal characterization and testing.

claim: Board cooling and cycle rate were increased by adding internal copper layers to the gripper boards outside of the microgripper region.
source: We additionally increased the board cooling and therefore cycle rate by adding internal copper layers to the gripper boards outside of the microgripper region.
evidence: This is a design modification implemented to improve performance.

claim: Step rates of 0.5 Hz (~300 μm/min) could be continuously maintained with steady-state board warming of a few degrees.
source: Step rates of 0.5 Hz (~300 μm/min) could be continuously maintained with steady-state board warming of a few degrees.
evidence: This is directly measured performance data for the device.

claim: Faster step rates of 2.5 Hz (~1.5 mm/min) could be maintained for brief periods of time.
source: Faster step rates of 2.5 Hz (~1.5 mm/min) could be maintained for brief periods of time.
evidence: This is directly measured performance data for the device.

claim: Greater timing flexibility and much faster step rates were possible when reduced numbers of probes were used, due to the reduced heat dissipation in the microgripper region.
source: Greater timing flexibility and, in particular, much faster step rates were also possible when reduced numbers of probes were used, due to the reduced heat dissipation in the microgripper region.
evidence: This is an observation from testing that is explained by thermal considerations.

claim: A tetrode moved using the maximum rated voltage for the piezo produced reliable stepwise motion as expected from the inchworm motor scheme.
source: A tetrode was first moved using the maximum rated voltage for the piezo, producing reliable stepwise motion as expected from the inchworm motor scheme (Figure 4B, top).
evidence: This is directly shown in the experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Step size can be decreased for finer resolution motion by reducing the voltage applied to the piezo during each step.
source: Step size can be decreased for finer resolution motion by reducing the voltage applied to the piezo during each step (Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: This is directly shown in the experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: The displacement of the probe matched the actuation distance of the piezo stack throughout the 100 V range of the driving signal.
source: The displacement of the probe matched the actuation distance of the piezo stack throughout the 100 V range of the driving signal (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: The minimum reliable step size was measured to be ~600 nm, near the limit of the optical resolving power.
source: The minimum reliable step size was measured to be ~600 nm, near the limit of our optical resolving power, and the maximum was 9.5 µm, corresponding to the stroke size of the piezo.
evidence: This is directly measured performance data for the device.

claim: The maximum step size was 9.5 µm, corresponding to the stroke size of the piezo.
source: The minimum reliable step size was measured to be ~600 nm, near the limit of our optical resolving power, and the maximum was 9.5 µm, corresponding to the stroke size of the piezo.
evidence: This is directly measured performance data for the device.

claim: A tetrode loaded into the microdrive and advanced by 9.5 µm steps exhibited a mean on-axis accuracy of 7 µm within a 1 mm total displacement range and 58 µm within a 4 mm total displacement range.
source: A tetrode loaded into the microdrive and advanced by 9.5 µm steps exhibited a mean on-axis accuracy of 7 µm within a 1 mm total displacement range and 58 µm within a 4 mm total displacement range (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured performance data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The tetrode loaded in the microdrive exhibited a mean repeatability of 38.3 µm (range: 5.5–106.1 µm, n=6 positions).
source: The tetrode loaded in the microdrive exhibited a mean repeatability of 38.3 µm (range: 5.5–106.1 µm, n=6 positions).
evidence: This is directly measured performance data.

claim: In an agar brain phantom, the repeatability improved to 4.7 µm (range: 0.9–12.9 µm, n=6 positions).
source: In an agar brain phantom, the repeatability improved to 4.7 µm (range: 0.9–12.9 µm, n=6 positions).
evidence: This is directly measured performance data.

claim: A possible cause for the improvement in repeatability in agar was the reduction of off-axis probe motion in the microgripper when the probe tip is constrained in the agar.
source: A possible cause for the improvement was the reduction of off-axis probe motion in the microgripper when the probe tip is constrained in the agar.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed improvement in repeatability.

claim: When both pipettes are in air, a single 9.5 µm step of the moving pipette caused the stationary one to move momentarily 3.6±2.1 µm on-axis and 23.8±4.4 µm (n=5 steps) off-axis.
source: When both pipettes are in air, a single 9.5 µm step of the moving pipette caused the stationary one to move momentarily 3.6±2.1 µm on-axis and 23.8±4.4 µm (n=5 steps) off-axis, i.e., laterally (Figure 4F 'cross-talk in air').
evidence: This is directly measured cross-talk data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Momentary deflections of a stationary probe are likely caused by a combination of thermal and phase change expansion of the PCM within the released bottom microgripper, lateral motion within the bore while released, and a non-straight and non-cylindrical probe sliding against the inner wall of this microgripper.
source: We reasoned that these momentary deflections of a stationary probe are likely caused by a combination of (1) thermal and phase change expansion of the PCM within the released bottom microgripper, (2) lateral motion within the bore while released, and (3) a non-straight and non-cylindrical probe (e.g. tetrode) sliding against the inner wall of this microgripper.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed cross-talk.

claim: When the cross-talk test was performed in an agar brain phantom, the stationary pipette moved significantly less (on-axis: 1.1±0.2 µm, p=0.03; off-axis: 0.85±0.2 µm, p<0.0001; n=5 steps).
source: As expected, when the same test was performed in an agar brain phantom, the stationary pipette moved significantly less (Figure 4F 'cross-talk in agar'; on-axis (x): 1.1±0.2 µm, p=0.03; off-axis (y): 0.85±0.2 µm, p<0.0001; n=5 steps; Student's unpaired t test).
evidence: This is directly measured cross-talk data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: After a moving tetrode was stepped continuously for 90 s (total distance of 500 µm), the stationary tetrode was found to have drifted less than 2 µm in x and y in air as well as in agar.
source: After the moving tetrode was stepped continuously for 90 s (total distance of 500 µm), the stationary one was found to have drifted less than 2 µm in x and y in air as well as in agar (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is directly measured drift data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The maximum weight that can be supported by the microdrive grip on a tetrode before the microgripper hold breaks was measured to be 58.0±2.4 g (n=5 tetrodes), equivalent to a holding force of 0.57 N.
source: Finally, the maximum weight that can be supported by the microdrive grip on a tetrode before the microgripper hold breaks was measured to be 58.0±2.4 g (n=5 tetrodes; Figure 4H), equivalent to a holding force of 0.57 N.
evidence: This is directly measured holding force data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: An integrated robotic microdrive for neural recordings with 16 twisted wire tetrode electrodes was assembled with an electrode interface and control board (EICB) with 64 recording channels (4 channels per each tetrode).
source: An integrated robotic microdrive for neural recordings with 16 twisted wire tetrode electrodes was assembled as shown schematically in Figure 5A, and in the photograph of Figure 5B. In addition to the main MPSA inchworm microdrive structure described previously, the complete design included an electrode interface and control board (EICB) with 64 recording channels (4 channels per each tetrode), connectors for extracellular recording amplifiers, electrode cannulas for maintaining electrode alignment, and a mechanical cage and mounts for encasing and positioning the drive for acute and chronic recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the assembled device shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The independent translation capability of the microdrive using only a single piezo actuator with 16 twisted wire tetrodes was demonstrated.
source: We again demonstrated the independent translation capability of the microdrive using only a single piezo actuator with 16 twisted wire tetrodes (Figure 5C, Video 4).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5C and Video 4.

claim: Independent translation of eight glass micropipettes (50 μm inner diameter/80 μm outer diameter) was demonstrated while only modifying the size of the heater coil (~100 μm inner diameter/135 μm outer diameter).
source: For the purposes of demonstrating this feature of the microdrive, in addition to neural twisted wire tetrode electrodes, we also independently translated eight glass micropipettes (50 μm inner diameter/80 μm outer diameter) while only modifying the size of the heater coil (~100 μm inner diameter/135 μm outer diameter) (Figure 5D–E, Video 5).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5D-E and Video 5.

claim: The neural recording capability of the microdrive was demonstrated in acute surgical settings on anesthetized rats, initially with 4 twisted wire tetrodes and then with 16 twisted wire tetrodes.
source: We first demonstrated the neural recording capability of our microdrive in acute surgical settings on anesthetized rats (see Materials and methods), initially with 4 twisted wire tetrodes (Video 6) and then with 16 twisted wire tetrodes as shown in Figure 6A.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6 and Video 6.

claim: Under remote operation, the electrodes were independently advanced in 9.5 μm steps sequentially into the brain, while 64 channels of neural signals were monitored visually to guide the approach of the tetrodes toward the targeted CA1 layer of the rat hippocampus.
source: Under remote operation, the electrodes (Figure 6B) were independently advanced in 9.5 μm steps sequentially into the brain, while 64 channels (from 16 tetrodes) of neural signals were monitored visually in order to guide the approach of the tetrodes toward the targeted CA1 layer of the rat hippocampus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure with results shown in Figure 6.

claim: In total, each probe moved ~2.5 mm, or ~250 steps each for a total of ~4200 step sequences within the experiment.
source: In total, each probe moved ~2.5 mm, or ~250 steps each for a total of ~4200 step sequences within the experiment.
evidence: This is a quantification of the total probe movement during the acute experiment.

claim: The microdrive produced only ~10 ms of interference within the spikeband after each step.
source: If done with a manual microdrive, this would have induced significant mechanical artifacts into the neural signal used for position feedback, whereas our device produced only ~10 ms of interference within the spikeband after each step (Appendix 1—figure 6), and ~0.1 s overall, allowing for rapid and ergonomic optimization.
evidence: This is directly measured artifact data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: There was no observed interference from the presence of the microdrive apart from the brief artifacts after each step.
source: Otherwise, there was no observed interference from the presence of the microdrive.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings.

claim: Tuning of additional tetrodes did not compromise the quality of the already placed tetrodes.
source: Importantly, tuning of additional tetrodes did not compromise the quality of the already placed tetrodes, as desired.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C where previously tuned tetrodes maintain signal quality.

claim: Chronic neural recording in an awake, unrestrained rat using an implantable tetrode-drive with four loaded tetrodes was performed.
source: As a final demonstration, we performed chronic neural recording in an awake, unrestrained rat using an implantable tetrode-drive with four loaded tetrodes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7.

claim: Before application of dental acrylic to cement the device to the skull, the overall weight was 4.5 g with overall dimensions of 25×15×31 mm.
source: Before application of dental acrylic to cement the device to the skull, the overall weight was 4.5 g with overall dimensions of 25×15×31 mm.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the device specifications.

claim: The weight and size would not have changed significantly if all 16 probes had been loaded: the overall structure would have remained the same, with the only additional weight coming from the 12 additional tetrodes and their connecting pins, grippers, and PCM, estimated to total approximately 10 mg.
source: As mentioned above, the weight and size would not have changed significantly if all 16 probes had been loaded: the overall structure would have remained the same, with the only additional weight coming from the 12 additional tetrodes and their connecting pins, grippers, and PCM, which we estimate to total approximately 10 mg (~50 mg if adding an optional intermediate spacer to reduce lateral bending of the flexible probes).
evidence: This is an estimate based on the design and component weights.

claim: The microdrive was maintained for 6 weeks, and the tetrode position was periodically adjusted through remote electronic control for fine-tuning of neural spike signal quality.
source: The microdrive was maintained for 6 weeks, and the tetrode position was periodically adjusted through remote electronic control for fine-tuning of neural spike signal quality.
evidence: This is a description of the chronic experiment duration and procedure.

claim: The recordings exhibited expected sharp-wave ripple and spiking activity.
source: The recordings exhibited expected sharp-wave ripple and spiking activity (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: During chronic implantations, a back-and-forth progression was used to advance the tetrodes to ensure minimal tissue movement after final probe alignment, leading to at least ~700 steps per probe and ~2800 steps for the microdrive.
source: During chronic implantations, a back-and-forth progression was used to advance the tetrodes to ensure minimal tissue movement after final probe alignment, leading to at least ~700 steps per probe and ~2800 steps for the microdrive.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and quantification of steps.

claim: During chronic experiments, the animal was only handled at the beginning and end of the measurement session, when the electrode and control cables were connected, and then all probe adjustments were controlled remotely through a computer.
source: Of particular importance was that, during these experiments, the animal was only handled at the beginning and end of the measurement session, when the electrode and control cables were connected, and then all probe adjustments were controlled remotely through a computer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure highlighting a key advantage of the device.

claim: Spike amplitudes and waveforms were stable during periods between successive tetrode adjustments, allowing isolation of multiple single units during free behavior in chronically implanted animals.
source: Spike amplitudes and waveforms were stable during periods between successive tetrode adjustments, allowing isolation of multiple single units during free behavior in chronically implanted animals (Figure 7E–F, Appendix 1—figure 7, and Methods).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7E-F and Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: The travel range of the MPSA microdrive is conceptually only limited by the length of the probe.
source: First, the travel range of the MPSA microdrive is conceptually only limited by the length of the probe.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the inchworm motor design with unlimited stepping capability.

claim: The MPSA microdrive could be used to simultaneously target distant regions of the brain (e.g. cortical and thalamic brain tissue) in large rodents or even primates.
source: Therefore, the MPSA microdrive could be used to simultaneously target distant regions of the brain (e.g. cortical and thalamic brain tissue) in large rodents or even primates (Dotson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential applications based on the long travel range capability.

claim: The MPSA concept makes the microdrive inherently more scalable than traditional microdrives.
source: Second, the MPSA concept makes the microdrive inherently more scalable than traditional microdrives.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the design comparison between MPSA and traditional microdrives.

claim: Each additional channel in a traditional motorized microdrive typically requires a motor, shuttle, and connector, causing the weight and size to increase substantially with channel count.
source: Each additional channel in a traditional motorized microdrive typically requires a motor, shuttle, and connector, causing the weight and size to increase substantially with channel count.
evidence: This is a statement about the design limitations of traditional microdrives based on established knowledge.

claim: In the MPSA microdrive, the addition of an extra channel causes a negligible weight and size increase, since the need for independent actuators is removed.
source: On the other hand, in the MPSA microdrive, the addition of an extra channel causes a negligible weight and size increase, since the need for independent actuators is removed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MPSA design and supported by weight measurements.

claim: Further improvements in scalability will rely on advances in the miniaturization of microchips and other electronic components, which is likely to outpace the miniaturization of traditional motors.
source: Third, further improvements in scalability will rely on advances in the miniaturization of microchips and other electronic components (e.g. higher-channel count current source integrated circuits), which is likely to outpace the miniaturization of traditional motors.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on trends in electronics miniaturization.

claim: Traditional microdrives utilize an inverted cone geometry in order to accommodate bulky actuators.
source: Fourth, traditional microdrives utilize an inverted cone geometry in order to accommodate bulky actuators.
evidence: This is a statement about the design of traditional microdrives based on established knowledge.

claim: The inverted cone geometry of traditional microdrives accommodates the use of flexible neural probes such as twisted-wire tetrodes and long silicon shanks but precludes the use of stiff micropipettes and short silicon shanks which are typically too inflexible to bend along the angular guide channel and through the vertical cannula.
source: This arrangement accommodates the use of flexible neural probes such as twisted-wire tetrodes and long silicon shanks (Michon et al., 2016) but precludes the use of stiff micropipettes and short silicon shanks which are typically too inflexible to bend along the angular guide channel and through the vertical cannula.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of traditional microdrive geometry based on mechanical constraints.

claim: Since the microgrippers in the MPSA microdrive can be tightly packed, the conical geometry is not needed, and rigid probes such as micropipettes can be translated.
source: Since the microgrippers in the MPSA microdrive can be tightly packed, the conical geometry is not needed, and rigid probes such as micropipettes can be translated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MPSA design and is demonstrated by the micropipette translation in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The releasing and gripping of the electrodes during stepping in the MPSA microdrive are gentle.
source: Another fundamental feature of the MPSA microdrive is that the releasing and gripping of the electrodes during stepping are gentle.
evidence: This is based on the mechanism of PCM melting and solidification without mechanical forces.

claim: The method of gripping and releasing is based on the melting and solidifying of the PCM around the electrode and inside the PCB via no matter what the shape or material of the electrode is.
source: The method is based on the melting and solidifying of the PCM around the electrode and inside the PCB via no matter what the shape or material of the electrode is (e.g. tetrode, glass capillary, silicon probe, and optical fiber).
evidence: This is a description of the gripping mechanism and is demonstrated with different probe types.

claim: The mechanism of gripping and releasing of electrodes ensures that there is no large or sudden gripper movement that might potentially damage the electrodes.
source: This mechanism of gripping and releasing of electrodes ensures that there is no large or sudden gripper movement (as would perhaps be expected from other mechanically based grippers) that might potentially damage the electrodes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the gentle nature of the gripping mechanism based on its design.

claim: During the course of the work, no mechanical or electrical damage to the recording electrodes was observed that compromised the electrical neural recordings.
source: During the course of our work, we have never observed any mechanical or electrical damage to the recording electrodes that in any way compromised our electrical neural recordings.
evidence: This is an observation from all the experiments conducted.

claim: During the motion of the electrodes in the MPSA device, the mechanism does not cause additional axial strain or compression on the electrodes.
source: It is also important to emphasize that during the motion of the electrodes in our device, as diagrammatically shown in Figure 2, the MPSA mechanism does not cause additional axial strain or compression on the electrodes, which would perhaps cause damage if they were.
evidence: This is explained by the stepping mechanism shown in Figure 2 where only one gripper holds at a time.

claim: During electrode motion while stepping, the electrode is only held by one and only one of the electrode grippers (either top or bottom) but never both.
source: During the electrode motion while stepping, the electrode is only held by one and only one of the electrode grippers (either top or bottom) but never both.
evidence: This is directly shown in the stepping sequence in Figure 2.

claim: Extension or contraction of the piezo actuator itself during motion never extends or contracts the electrode itself.
source: Therefore, extension or contraction of our piezo actuator itself during motion never extends or contracts the electrode itself.
evidence: This is a consequence of the stepping mechanism where only one gripper holds at a time.

claim: The electrodes held and positioned by the MPSA device are never fully loose while being translated; they are always gripped by at least one gripper at any one time during translation.
source: Furthermore, the electrodes held and positioned by our device are never fully loose while being translated. They are always gripped by at least one gripper at any one time during translation, as Figure 2 describes.
evidence: This is directly shown in the stepping sequence in Figure 2.

claim: Minimal thermal design is required for a single probe implementation but coupling and heat flow become more important as the probe count and heater density increase.
source: Minimal thermal design is required for a single probe implementation but coupling and heat flow become more important as the probe count and heater density increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from thermal characterization and simulations.

claim: The relevant thermal phenomena can be readily modeled with heat transfer simulations.
source: The relevant phenomena, however, can be readily modeled with heat transfer simulations, and we envision that more sophisticated mechanical and control schemes could yield higher probe densities and movement speeds (see Appendix 1 for additional details).
evidence: This is based on the simulations performed and described in the Materials and methods and Appendix.

claim: More sophisticated mechanical and control schemes could yield higher probe densities and movement speeds.
source: The relevant phenomena, however, can be readily modeled with heat transfer simulations, and we envision that more sophisticated mechanical and control schemes could yield higher probe densities and movement speeds (see Appendix 1 for additional details).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential improvements based on the current understanding.

claim: Increasing the movement speed is important for generalizing the use of these temperature-sensitive PCM-based grippers, as many applications require faster rates than utilized in the current work.
source: In particular, increasing the movement speed is important for generalizing the use of these temperature-sensitive PCM-based grippers, as many applications require faster rates than utilized here.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current implementation and future needs.

claim: Examples of more advanced methods to improve performance include integrating copper heat sink regions between microgrippers and optimizing heating timings based on the mutual impulse response and heating history of all the thermally coupled heaters on a board.
source: Examples of more advanced methods include integrating copper heat sink regions between microgrippers and optimizing heating timings based on the mutual impulse response and heating history of all the thermally coupled heaters on a board.
evidence: These are proposed improvements based on thermal engineering principles.

claim: The PCM could be chosen for the temperature of the application or designed to have properties helpful to the microgripper functionality such as higher thermal diffusivity and a narrower phase transition.
source: Additionally, the PCM could be chosen for the temperature of the application or designed to have properties helpful to the microgripper functionality such as higher thermal diffusivity and a narrower phase transition (Hyun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential material improvements with a citation to relevant work.

claim: The heating of the brain due to operation of the MPSA device is essentially negligible.
source: It is important to emphasize that the heating of the brain due to operation of our device is essentially negligible.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of heating duration, thermal resistance, and PCM temperature.

claim: During the robotic stepping of the device for electrode translation, the heating pulse required for melting of the phase change grippers is extremely short (~10 ms), while the piezo actuator's steps are ~1 s long.
source: During the robotic stepping of the device for electrode translation, described in Figure 2, the heating pulse required for melting of the phase change grippers is extremely short (~10 ms), while the piezo actuator's steps (which do not generate heat) are ~1 s long.
evidence: This is based on the timing parameters shown in Figure 2 and described in the characterization section.

claim: The heaters in any of the PCBs of the MPSA device are on for only up to 1% of the overall stepping motion time.
source: Therefore, the heaters in any of the PCBs of our device are on for only up to 1% of the overall stepping motion time.
evidence: This is calculated from the heating pulse duration and step duration.

claim: The small amount of heat energy generated by the heaters within the PCB vias is rapidly dissipated within the large PCB volume and does not thermally conduct to the brain through the very large thermal resistance of the microscopic recording electrodes.
source: Additionally, that small amount of heat energy generated by the heaters within the PCB vias is (by design of the copper layers of the PCB) rapidly dissipated within the large PCB volume and does not thermally conduct to the brain through the very large thermal resistance of the microscopic recording electrodes.
evidence: This is based on thermal design principles and the physical properties of the materials.

claim: The PCM for the MPSA device was chosen so that the grippers would not need to rise to a temperature significantly above the typical temperature of the brain.
source: Furthermore, the PCM for this device was chosen so that the grippers would not need to rise to a temperature significantly above the typical temperature of the brain.
evidence: This is a design choice based on the melting temperature of docosane (~42°C) relative to brain temperature.

claim: During the electrode recordings from neurons, or simply during the idle state of the device, all the electrodes are fixed (gripped) in the device, which by design occurs when all the heaters in the device are off and generate no heat.
source: Finally, during the electrode recordings from neurons, or simply during the idle state of the device, all the electrodes are fixed (gripped) in the device, which by design occurs when all the heaters in the device are off and generate no heat.
evidence: This is a consequence of the gripping mechanism where solid PCM grips without heating.

claim: Electrical pick-up artifacts during electrode motion are of potential concern with nearby applied voltages, electrical currents through the microheaters, and repeated piezo actuation steps.
source: Electrical pick-up artifacts during electrode motion are also of potential concern, as is to be expected with nearby applied voltages, electrical currents through the microheaters in the PCB vias that surround the recording electrodes, and repeated piezo actuation steps (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is a potential problem identified based on the electrical operation of the device.

claim: Electrical recordings from neurons with sensitive neural amplifiers coupled to the electrodes were regularly performed during the stepping motion of the device without apparent issue to the tissue or electronics.
source: However, the electrical recordings from neurons with sensitive neural amplifiers coupled to the electrodes were regularly performed during the stepping motion of the device without apparent issue to the tissue or electronics.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: It was never necessary to disconnect or power down the elements of the device that perform the motion steps to improve the data quality.
source: It was never necessary to disconnect or power down the elements of the device that perform the motion steps (piezo actuator and the heaters) to improve the data quality, but if motion was not being performed during a recording session, it was also not necessary to use or power these elements.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: The MPSA mechanism does not affect the ability to perform effective neural recordings.
source: Therefore, the described MPSA mechanism in no way affects the ability to perform effective neural recordings.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful neural recordings obtained in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Recordings can be taken with high fidelity after each motion step of only ~10 microns or less, and this mechanism is likely to yield improved recording quality.
source: As recordings can be taken with high fidelity after each motion step of only ~10 microns or less, this mechanism is instead likely to yield improved recording quality.
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated recording quality and the ability to make fine adjustments.

claim: The MPSA microdrive design is particularly attractive for rodent electrophysiology where miniaturization is critical.
source: While this MPSA microdrive design is particularly attractive for rodent electrophysiology where miniaturization is critical, in other uses, weight and size can be traded for additional functionality.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated miniaturization and successful rodent experiments.

claim: In situations where motion accuracy is critical, a positional feedback system such as a small camera could be installed.
source: For example, in situations where motion accuracy is critical, a positional feedback system such as a small camera could be installed.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential improvements.

claim: An MRI compatible version of the microdrive would be a particularly interesting variant of imaging feedback control, as the design does not require ferrous components.
source: Alternatively, the design does not require ferrous components, and therefore an MRI compatible version of the microdrive (Matsui et al., 2007) would be a particularly interesting variant of imaging feedback control.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the materials used in the device with a citation to relevant work.

claim: Further directions for the implantable neural MPSA microdrive include enabling untethered control and recordings through wireless communication via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, implementing on-board piezoelectric drivers and battery-powered operation.
source: Further directions for the implantable neural MPSA microdrive include enabling untethered control and recordings through wireless communication via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, implementing on-board piezoelectric drivers and battery-powered operation.
evidence: These are forward-looking statements about potential future developments.

claim: An important advancement to the functionality would be the implementation of autonomous probe positioning.
source: An important advancement to the functionality would be the implementation of autonomous probe positioning.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential improvements.

claim: Computer-controlled closed loop spike detection and fidelity monitoring capabilities would allow for the placement of a probe within a region of interest based upon a model signal and thereafter optimization of signal quality.
source: While in our demonstrations the operator was involved in the probe positioning, computer-controlled closed loop spike detection and fidelity monitoring capabilities would allow for the placement of a probe within a region of interest based upon a model signal and thereafter optimization of signal quality, in which degradation could trigger automatic compensatory motion (Cham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential automation with a citation to relevant work.

claim: Automation of probe positioning could lead to both improved data yield and reduced operator time in experiments.
source: Such automation could lead to both improved data yield and reduced operator time in experiments.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the benefits of automation.

claim: Apart from neural electrophysiology probes, the MPSA microdrive could also be used for other biological as well as non-biological probe translation tasks.
source: Apart from neural electrophysiology probes, the MPSA microdrive could also be used for other biological as well as non-biological probe translation tasks (Matsui et al., 2007; Sych et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential applications with citations to relevant work.

claim: The microgrippers could be sized to accommodate hypodermic needles, optical fibers, and ultrasonic transducers and sensors on a variety of scales.
source: For example, the microgrippers could be sized to accommodate hypodermic needles, optical fibers, and ultrasonic transducers and sensors on a variety of scales.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential applications based on the demonstrated versatility.

claim: For larger diameter probes, minimizing the amount of PCM within the via between the probe and the helical heater coil would be important to reduce the required heat to melt the PCM, reduce the lateral motion of the probe during translation, and maintain the capillary action that keeps the PCB within the via.
source: For any of these larger diameter probes, minimizing the amount of PCM within the via between the probe and the helical heater coil would be important. This would reduce the required heat to melt the PCM, reduce the lateral motion of the probe during translation, and maintain the capillary action that keeps the PCB within the via.
evidence: This is a design consideration for scaling to larger probes based on the principles of the current design.

claim: With larger probes, there is an additional consideration of the amount of heat the probe itself can conduct away from the gripper based on the probe's cross-section and thermal diffusivity characteristics.
source: With larger probes, there becomes an additional consideration of the amount of heat the probe itself can conduct away from the gripper. This is based on the probe's cross-section and thermal diffusivity characteristics, where a very thermally diffusive probe might require modifications to the process (such as higher power and a relatively longer melting time) in order to fully melt the PCM in the via.
evidence: This is a design consideration for scaling to larger probes based on thermal physics principles.

claim: The robotic microdrive provides the capability for independent positioning of multiple parallel probes using only a single piezo actuator with significant benefits wherever the need arises for small weight, miniature device size, sub-micron level probe positioning precision, and remote control.
source: In conclusion, our robotic microdrive provides the capability for independent positioning of multiple parallel probes using only a single piezo actuator with significant benefits wherever the need arises for small weight, miniature device size, sub-micron level probe positioning precision, and remote control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the demonstrated capabilities of the device.

claim: Heating coils were prepared by winding fine insulated nichrome wire around a 75 μm diameter tungsten wire core.
source: Heating coils were prepared by winding fine insulated nichrome wire (California Fine Wire, Model Stableohm 800 A, 12.5 μm diameter conductor, 17.5 μm diameter with insulation) around a 75 μm diameter tungsten wire core (California Fine Wire).
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication method.

claim: The final microheater had ~45 turns and had a typical resistance of 125 Ω for a tetrode microgripper.
source: The final microheater had ~45 turns, as shown in Figure 1C, and had a typical resistance of 125 Ω for a tetrode microgripper.
evidence: This is a specification of the fabricated component shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Docosane was chosen as the PCM due to its non-toxicity and sharp, low melting temperature (~42℃), which is still above animal body temperature.
source: Docosane (Sigma-Aldrich, item 134457) was chosen as the PCM due to its non-toxicity and sharp, low melting temperature (~42℃), which is still above animal body temperature (Balaban et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a design choice with justification and a citation.

claim: Gripper board designs were simulated in COMSOL Multiphysics before fabrication in order to implement a design with sufficient microgripper thermal independence.
source: The gripper board designs were simulated in COMSOL Multiphysics before fabrication in order to implement a design with sufficient microgripper thermal independence (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the design process using simulation.

claim: Gripper boards were manufactured using standard PCB technology with specifications of 8×11×0.8 mm, six layers.
source: Gripper boards were manufactured using standard PCB technology (8×11×0.8 mm, six layers, Sierra Circuits).
evidence: This is a specification of the manufactured component.

claim: To increase the microgripper and overall board cooling rate, solid internal layers and thermal vias in the non-gripper regions of the board were used to increase the thermal conduction across the plane and through the thickness of the board.
source: To increase the microgripper and overall board cooling rate (and therefore the cycle rate), solid internal layers and thermal vias (~27 per cm2) in the non-gripper regions of the board were used to increase the thermal conduction across the plane and through the thickness of the board, respectively (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of a design feature to improve thermal performance.

claim: Building the core MPSA motor and developing the control software are in principle possible for a typical system neuroscience-focused laboratory.
source: Building the core MPSA motor – the grippers, piezo, and board assembly – and developing the control software are in principle possible for a typical system neuroscience-focused laboratory.
evidence: This is a statement about the accessibility of the technology.

claim: In the research and development laboratory setting, construction of the entire device takes about 1 week of labor for a trained person.
source: In our practice in a research and development laboratory setting, a construction of the entire device takes about 1 week of labor for a trained person.
evidence: This is a practical observation about the fabrication time.

claim: Once the MPSA motor is constructed, it is reusable, and the preparation time of the microdrive for experimental use is only required for reloading of the recording electrodes.
source: However, once the MPSA motor is constructed, it is reusable, and the preparation time of the microdrive for experimental use is only required for reloading of the recording electrodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the reusability of the device based on its design.

claim: All procedures involving animals were performed according to methods approved by the Janelia Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures involving animals were performed according to methods approved by the Janelia Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: All acute surgical experiments were performed on anesthetized Wistar male rats (age: P20–P30).
source: All acute surgical experiments were performed on anesthetized Wistar male rats (age: P20–P30).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: To record from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer, probes were advanced approximately 2.5 mm from the surface of the cortex.
source: To record from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer, probes were advanced approximately 2.5 mm from the surface of the cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The cells in the CA1 pyramidal cell layer produce pronounced and distinct burst patterns and remain relatively active under anesthesia.
source: The cells in this layer produce pronounced and distinct burst patterns and remain relatively active under anesthesia.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of CA1 neurons based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Electrodes progressing toward the CA1 cell layer pass through regions with characteristic activity patterns.
source: Furthermore, electrodes progressing toward the cell layer pass through regions with characteristic activity patterns.
evidence: This is a statement about hippocampal anatomy and physiology based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: For chronic recordings, Long-Evans rats were used.
source: For chronic recordings, Long-Evans rats were first anesthetized with isoflurane and headfixed in a stereotaxic frame.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects for chronic recordings.

claim: The tetrode tips were gold-plated to reduce the impedance of each channel to <250 kΩ at 1 kHz.
source: The tetrode tips were previously gold-plated to reduce the impedance of each channel to <250 kΩ at 1 kHz, and a stainless steel screw placed in contact with the left cerebellum served as the reference electrode for recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode preparation procedure.

claim: Eleven single units were isolated from the 4 tetrodes in the chronic recording.
source: We isolated 11 single units from the 4 tetrodes.
evidence: This is a quantification of the neural recording results.
